passages.text: The nature of the one and only God, who made the world, created us, and provided everything, is naturally such that, whenever anyone at all is within the bounds of reverence for God and does not blaspheme his holy spirit, it carries that person’s soul toward him by affection for him, in the form of an innate longing for him. Even if that person is a sinner, after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved. If someone denies him or in some other way speaks impiously against him, then repents, he will indeed be punished for the ways in which he sinned against him, but he will be saved, because after turning back he loved him. Perhaps, however, if there is an extraordinary degree of reverence and supplication, he will even be released from punishment, having presented his ignorance together with his repentance as grounds for forgiveness of the sin. Those, however, who have not repented will also meet their end through the punishment of fire, even if they are most devout in every other respect. But, as I said, after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age, they will be extinguished. For those who have acted impiously against the eternal and only God can no longer exist forever.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the repeated nature language of πέφυκεν and φύσις while allowing the following infinitive to express what this nature characteristically does.
Preserves the possessive expression and descriptive wording without using English capitalization to settle personhood beyond what the Greek itself marks.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ὧν ἔπραξεν κολασθῆναι σώζεσθαι φύσιν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ ἀξίαν expresses punishment corresponding to the worth or deserts of the deeds, while φύσιν ἔχει continues the passage’s emphasis on nature.

The response follows denial or impious speech and precedes the stated turning back and love, supporting moral-spiritual repentance under the October13 contextual policy. The later noun and negated participle receive the same cognate repentance terminology. The distinct ἐπιστρέψας remains after turning back rather than being merged with repent. No destination or intensifier is added, and the historical author's stated punishment-and-salvation framework is left intact.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συγγνώμης τῆς ἁμαρτίας μετὰ τῆς μετανοίας δεδωκὼς τὴν ἄγνοιαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: having presented his ignorance together with his repentance as grounds for forgiveness of the sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact construction presents ignorance and repentance in relation to pardon. It may alternatively be understood as offering ignorance as an excuse for the sin, but the chosen wording preserves both elements without making ignorance itself absolve him. Repentance reflects the morally responsive context rather than a mere change of opinion; no new condition or causal formula is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μεμετρημένου αἰῶνος τὸ πέμπτον πυρὶ αἰωνίῳ κολασθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Age-long” preserves the relation between αἰωνίῳ and αἰῶνος and fits the explicitly measured duration. “Eternal fire” is a possible lexical alternative, in which case the fire rather than each person’s punishment would be described as eternal.
Preserves the image of something being put out rather than replacing it with an interpretive abstraction such as “annihilated.”

source_issues.source_quote: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος
source_issues.issue: The confirmed selected print has smooth-breathed οὐδήποτε, ordinarily never. That negative reading is syntactically possible: substantival παντός can supply the person in a genitive absolute, while never modifies ὄντος, giving an alternative such as any person who is never within the bounds of reverence for God. The positive main text instead follows the explicitly proposed genitive indefinite οὑδήποτε, of anyone whatsoever. The surrounding coordinated nonblasphemy, reverence, and innate longing favor describing a reverently disposed person, motivating the proposed breathing interpretation, but do not make the supplied negative construction grammatically impossible. The proposed positive reading remains distinct from the confirmed printed negative; no change to the Greek, newly verified corrected reading, or recovery of unique original wording is claimed.
source_issues.proposed_reading: παντὸς οὑδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος

source_issues.issue: The confirmed printed raised dot interrupts the natural construction in which ἰδέᾳ governs the preceding genitive phrase. Treating it as sentence-final would leave ἰδέᾳ isolated before the full stop. The translation therefore provisionally treats the raised dot as anomalous internal editorial punctuation and attaches ἰδέᾳ to the preceding words.

passages.text: For this reason, after first being deceived by Simon the forerunner, you died to God in your souls, and your bodies were struck. But likewise, a second time, through repentance—as I said—by accepting what pleases God, you can both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls. What pleases God is this: to pray to him; to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law; to abstain from “the table of demons”; not to taste dead flesh; not to touch blood; and to wash oneself clean of every pollution. As for the rest, hear it, all of you, in one saying, just as the Jews who revere God have heard it, taking up one mind in many bodies: “Whatever good things each person wants for himself, he should plan the same things for his neighbor as well.” Each of you would understand what is good in this way, if he were to reason with himself as follows: “You do not want to be murdered; do not murder another. You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife. You do not want any of your possessions to be stolen; do not steal anything belonging to another.” And so, recognizing from your own case what is reasonable and doing it, you will become dear to God and obtain healing; for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age and punished in your souls in the age to come.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after first being deceived by Simon the forerunner
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόδρομος explicitly calls Simon a forerunner, while προαπατάω presents the deception as prior; the translation does not specify whose forerunner he is.

The context concerns a moral-spiritual response expressed in accepting the things pleasing to God, so repentance follows the October13 contextual policy. The existing through relation, ensuing bodily and soul restoration, and the historical writer's practices are preserved rather than replaced by a new canonical formula. No extra destination or intensifier is inserted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὰ σώματα ἀναρρῶσαι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀναλαβεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναρρωννύω denotes renewed bodily strength, while ἀναλαμβάνω here presents the souls as regained or recovered; “take up your souls again” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν αἰτεῖν ὡς πάντα νόμῳ κριτικῷ διδόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law
lexical_decisions.rationale: κριτικός can mean discriminating or judicial. “According to a law of discernment” is possible, but the surrounding emphasis on consequences and punishment favors “judicial.”
The wording directly prohibits tasting flesh that is dead; it has not been generalized to a familiar dietary formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν πολλοῖς σώμασιν μίαν γνώμην ἀναλαβόντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: taking up one mind in many bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the author’s image of bodily plurality united in a single judgment or disposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ θέλεις τὴν σὴν ὑφ’ ἑτέρου μοιχευθῆναι γυναῖκα, τὴν ἑτέρου μὴ μοίχευε γαμετήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English changes the first clause from passive to active to avoid implying sexual coercion while preserving the participants and the repeated adultery terminology. The distinction between γυναῖκα, “wife,” and γαμετήν, “wedded wife,” is also retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τῷ παρόντι αἰῶνι βασανισθήσεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age
lexical_decisions.rationale: After an exhortation or stated favorable outcome, ἐπεί can introduce the consequence that follows otherwise. The formally possible “since indeed you will be tormented” would obscure the warning contrast supplied by the context.

The nominative plural participle supplies the subordinate circumstance or means under which the restoration is possible. Having accepted what pleases God is a temporal-circumstantial alternative. The finite you can governs the two later infinitives, restore and recover, not a third coordinate ability to accept. The present repentance wording and the historical author's stated practices remain intact; no additional canonical formula is supplied.
